newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovakia moves to stop privatisation bond slide.
newsitem.headline: Slovakia moves to stop privatisation bond slide.

text.p: Slovakian authorities are trying to shore up their ailing privatisation bonds market by enforcing a minimum selling price to prevent investors trading far below official values.
Slovakia's RMS over-the-counter bourse said on Thursday it would take measures forcing citizens to sell the bonds at a minimum official price.

A shortage of ready buyers means citizens desperate for cash have been willing to sell at knock-down prices in private deals rather than waiting often several months or even indefinitely to find a buyer through the RMS system at the minimum price.

The bonds have a nominal value of 10,000 crowns and the government has guaranteed a minimum price for trading of 7,500 crowns, but have been changing hands in large volumes at prices significantly below the minimum.
While the Slovak government is officially committed to the free market it often resorts to "administrative measures" or regulation to tackle problems such as collapsing bond prices.

"From Monday, all direct deals with privatisation bonds will have to be financially settled through the RMS, to guarantee that the minimum price of 7,500 crowns has been observed," Peter Krupa, a senior official at the RM-System (RMS) bourse, told Reuters.

On Tuesday Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar expressed his disappointment over the privatisation bond programme, launched in August to replace the second wave of mass "voucher privatisation" which his government halted last year.
Trading of the bonds kicked off to much fanfare but little else as thousands of Slovaks lined up to sell the paper, issued by the state privatisation agency, the National Property Fund.
Meciar blamed Privatisation Minister Peter Bisak for the shaky start to the programme, and called the current levels at which the bonds were trading a crime.
"The premier said trade with the bonds at 3,500, or even 2,500 crowns, can only be called daylight robbery," Meciar's spokeswoman Magda Pospisilova said.
Krupa admitted that the new settlement rule could not be watertight. "From Monday, every deal must be settled through a special, so-called 'jumbo' account," he said.
"Of course, we cannot say all those who want to get round the law are prevented from doing it, but we assume it will be at least harder for them," he added.
The bonds, which can be redeemed only in five years, were issued to about 3.3 million Slovaks in place of the cancelled second wave of voucher privatisation.

The first wave, launched in 1992 shortly before the former Czechoslovakia split in two, proved exceptionally popular. More than two thirds of the Slovak population registered for the second wave when Meciar was briefly in opposition in 1994.

But when he regained power at the end of that year he first suspended the scheme, under which citizens use vouchers issued at a nominal cost to bid for shares in state companies, and later cancelled it completely.

The privatisation bonds have a floating interest rate equal to the discount rate, currently 8.8 percent. Proceeds of direct privatisation sales to professional investors are supposed to fund the bonds.
As of September 30, only 1,590 bonds had been traded in anonymous over-the-counter auctions and 70,515 bonds were sold directly, mostly at a price equal or close to 7,500 crowns.

But difficulty in selling the bonds and a lack of trust in the scheme has pushed many Slovaks to sell the bonds at almost any price. Until now, direct deals on the RMS have been allowed also with financial settlement outside the bourse system, enabling trading at the prices below the official price.
